title: SHE REVERENCE HER HUSBAND: Submission, Grace & Self-Examination of a Biblical Wife

sense.text:
“It is not good that the man should be alone; I will make him an help meet for him.” Here the woman’s original function in marriage was set: a help meet. He did not say I will make him a romantic lover, or I will make him a baby factory. The first thing a man needs, and the reason a union is joined, is that spiritual, biblical help meet. There is no other reason before it; the rest of the scriptures flesh out and build on what a wife is.

Many women seek a husband for money, and that is not wrong in itself. That was part of the old values: a woman married because there was an opportunity for her and she needed certain things from the man, not holding off marriage till thirty, having fun in college (playing the hoe) and then getting married. But the number one thing in a woman’s mind when she seeks to marry according to God should be to be that man’s help meet. When she is proving a man, that should be one of her chief desires.

Sisters say yes, they are ready to be submissive, and they are not. They are thinking about the rod, about somebody to watch Netflix with; that is why they start fixing plates two months in, trying to seduce him. Many think that because they’ve got the box for their man, that is all they need to bring to the table. When the honeymoon is over and he has gotten his fill of the vagina, a man filled with purpose has other things he wants to focus on. That doesn’t mean he forgets about wanting sex; sex nourishes the marriage, but it slows down and spaces out, at least for a man who is about putting in work. A man who spends all his time chasing box, even his wife’s, is up under her skirt, and God called us for more. Then he starts to see the kinks in the armour, what is lacking in the marriage. A year or two later she realises, too late, that she got married because she wanted warmth.

Being a help meet does not make a woman unintelligent, voiceless or incapable. Proverbs 31 destroys that caricature: the virtuous woman is capable and intelligent, extraordinarily strong, and brings value to the relationship and the family, and women should strive for that. You can’t build a family without the woman, and a woman can’t be the dad and everything else; there is an interdependency. But her strength operates with order. She has her role, her strength and the gifts God gave her to fulfil in the nation and in the marriage, but it has to be with order.

precepts.why:
The help meet’s strength has to operate in order, and this is the order: “the head of every man is Christ; and the head of the woman is the man; and the head of Christ is God.” God, Christ, man, woman. Christians call it headship. There is always a head; even the scriptures speak of the Godhead.

This order does not mean the husband has it all together, that he is always right, or that he is always emotionally mature. There are no qualifiers on it. Sisters say the men don’t see Christ in them yet, don’t value them that way yet, but the order is not contingent on that. It is not following him only when she agrees with his decision. It is the order God set from the foundation of the earth.

It is like faith: easy to have when everything is good, but when things become challenging, that is when faith is magnified. Agreement doesn’t require submission. A wife knows whether she has a submissive spirit precisely when she has a different opinion from how her husband wants to lead. That is when she sees whose authority she is really under.

So a husband is not his wife’s improvement project. She is his wife, not his supervisor. It is not her job to fix him or to teach him: Christ is the head of every man, Christ deals with him and Christ will get him right. Some wives call it helping, but every suggestion carries correction, even said with sweet words after rubbing his shoulder; every question challenges his judgment; every conversation tells him how he could have done better. Women are the most critical of both genders; they even criticise one another with compliments. Eventually he stops hearing concern and hears constant dissatisfaction, as if nothing he does can be received without being evaluated. That is not submission and it is not being led.

Being a helper does not mean managing the man she was created to support. Help strengthens; control supervises, and reverence for her husband is what teaches a wife the difference. She should ask herself honestly: does my husband experience me as a woman who believes in him, or as another person he must continually prove himself to? Men are always proving themselves, at work, in the street, among other men; it is built into the masculine frame. A man married her because of what the Bible says, for a help meet and a submissive wife, and he comes home to unwind in a safe place, not to measure up to one more person.

sense.text:
“I will greatly multiply thy sorrow and thy conception; in sorrow thou shalt bring forth children”: here God starts adding things to the marriage, the labour pains. Then: “thy desire shall be to thy husband, and he shall rule over thee.”

Desire is intense wanting, seeking. A woman’s natural inclination should be to have her husband as her hedge, and a desire to keep that man happy in any way possible, because she wants her husband’s approval. That is very different from trying to fix him and making him her project.

That strong desire is an acknowledgment that he is responsible for her well-being, her safety and her nurturing. The fact that he provides those things without any conditions should guarantee a fervent desire to please him and have a mind after him. The trad wife said she doesn’t have to think: the man leads, the woman follows. It doesn’t get any simpler than that. When marriages go away from it they suffer, because it is against nature as God intended marriage to be: “he shall rule over thee.”

This is where submission starts: her desire shall be to her husband. A wife adapts to her husband, not the other way around. She can never submit to a husband she will not adapt to; if she is trying to make him adapt to her, she will always have resentment and bitterness inside.

Read as a whole letter, Ephesians focuses heavily on God’s plan to bring all things united under Christ. He made known “the mystery of his will”: “That in the dispensation of the fulness of times he might gather together in one all things in Christ, both which are in heaven, and which are on earth; even in him.” Unity: gathering all things into one.

In chapters 1 to 3 Paul shows that plan being carried out: the middle wall of partition broken down between the northern and southern kingdom, and now one new man in Christ. In chapters 4 to 6 he applies it: living out the unity of the spirit in the congregation, in personal daily conduct, and especially in the household. So when he reaches Ephesians 5:22 and on, marriage represents the relationship between Christ and the church, the same order as 1 Corinthians 11:3; then he touches the children; and in chapter 6 he tells marriages, households, congregations and individuals to put on armour against whatever would break down that unity of all things under Christ.

That is what makes his marriage argument so strong. Submission, love, reverence, grace and self-examination are not only for marriage; they apply to every one of us in this walk, and they show what life is going to be in the kingdom of heaven. If you can’t be faithful in those things here on earth, how can you be an heir of them in the kingdom? Biblical marriage is not about men trying to dominate women. It is God’s order, so that all things can be brought under Christ, quite literally.

“Submitting yourselves one to another in the fear of God.” The fear of God means as God said the responsibilities are. Marriage is not 50/50, except in this: the woman is 100% responsible for her role as God says it, and that is her submission to the man; the man is responsible for his submission to Christ, following what Christ says he is to do and be as a husband.

So verse 21 does not mean the husband submits to his wife. Right away Paul establishes the order again.

“Wives, submit yourselves unto your own husbands, as unto the Lord.” As unto the Lord.

Submission is the act of yielding control to a more powerful or authoritative entity. A wife who puts qualifications on it, whose submission requires him first to understand what she is dealing with and going through, has yet to be in submission. There is a place for that understanding, but it is his job to see when that place is, not hers to make her submission conditional on it.

Submission is willingly placing yourself under authority and order. It is not inferiority. It is powerful, because it is magnified in the willing spirit it is done with; done grudgingly, it is not submission, and she will never find the peace that comes through it. How can we say we want one nation in Christ, one people ruling the whole earth, and live in division in our marriages? Whoever doesn’t practise that submission isn’t worthy of the kingdom, because they don’t know how to serve.

Submission is also submitting something for approval. Her desire unto him means she wants her husband’s approval and acknowledgment, and it should come because he sees it in her actions, her chaste conversation.

“For the husband is the head of the wife, even as Christ is the head of the church: and he is the saviour of the body.” Her desire unto him is the acknowledgment of his nurturing, his protection, the hedge he provides; he is the saviour of the body, and she needs to see it that way. The body is her and him together as one flesh, and their household, which is a reflection of a little nation.

“Therefore as the church is subject unto Christ, so let the wives be to their own husbands in every thing.” The wife is the church in this similitude: the same way the church is subject to Christ is exactly the way she is to be subject to her husband.

In everything, short of sin. A husband cannot tell her to sin and make it right; we ought to obey God rather than men. But anything else he tells her to do, she does: no rebuttals, no contestation.

“And the wife see that she reverence her husband.” Reverence is a feeling of deep respect tinged with awe; veneration. It is deep respect expressed in attitude, in speech, and most of all in conduct. Some sisters’ words come out sweet while their face is a war face. The Greek word here, phobeo, is that reverencing and respecting of the husband in the relationship, and reverence is also the outward manifestation of that feeling: she has to show it. Saying but I do is not enough.

A wife should look at her husband with awe, the same way she did when she was proving him and couldn’t wait to see him. Many wives barely get up when the husband comes home; the dog is more excited to see him than the wife, and the kids and pets greet him at the door more than she does.

“Let every one of you in particular so love his wife even as himself”: that love is agape. It is not romantic love: not sit down and cuddle me, take me on dates. It is the love God and Christ have for his people, the love of one person for another without sexual implications, marked by a committed concern for the other’s good: a sacrificial love, as Christ gave himself for the church.

A man sacrifices a lot when he marries and has children; he puts the family before others and before his own well-being. It is thankless. Its reward should be the biblical marriage itself, but in modern times men are still expected to give that sacrificial love without the benefits it was given for. Romantic, affectionate love comes by nurturing, by how a wife behaves; nobody wants to take a wife out who is nasty all the time.

So marriage is not coexisting until you drop dead or Christ returns. It is a high standard for both: the wife is called to submission and reverence, and the husband is commanded to love sacrificially, to nourish and cherish his wife the way Christ gave his life.

precepts.why:
Reverence shows in rising up: the scripture says to rise up before the hoary head, the senior. Here she said to her father, “Let it not displease my lord that I cannot rise up before thee; for the custom of women is upon me.” She would not get up before him because, she said, she had her period. “And he searched, but found not the images.”

It was an evil thing she did: she was sitting on idolatrous images she had stolen. But the custom shows what reverence looked like: a woman rose up before her lord to honour him. So how often does a wife greet her husband at the door? It doesn’t happen.

Husbands are to love their wives, and the scripture speaks of cleaving: “Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh.” To cleave is to adhere closely, stick, cling; to remain faithful. It means very closely joined, and remaining firmly attached.

Cleaving makes a new household. A married couple shouldn’t be living in mama’s house or daddy’s house (outside of something catastrophic); they should have their own roof. That is why Bishop Nathanyel always says a strong marriage, run by biblical principles with both sides playing their part, is the foundation for a strong nation.

Cleaving means allegiance shifts. As much as she loves her dad and her mom, she is now under the authority of her husband; it is about this new household now. An over-attachment of allegiance to mom and dad can happen on both the husband’s and the wife’s side.

Think of two pieces of wood glued so tightly that if you try to pull them apart they won’t come apart cleanly; the wood splinters and pieces of each stay on the other. That is how close the cleaving is. Husband and wife function as one, a team: one affects the other, for good or for bad.

Paul paraphrases Genesis: “For this cause shall a man leave his father and mother, and shall be joined unto his wife, and they two shall be one flesh. This is a great mystery: but I speak concerning Christ and the church.” Then verse 33 again: let every one “so love his wife even as himself; and the wife see that she reverence her husband.”

Marriage is not just a social contract, as they say. It is a literal symbolism of Christ and the church on the earth. Ephesians is about unity, everything coming under one in Christ, both kingdoms, northern and southern, and how we must endeavour to keep that unity. That is what makes the submission on the wife’s part so critical.

The wives are pressed on because most men are fulfilling the overarching primary functions of a man, and how much harder that becomes when it is done for someone ungrateful and disrespectful. Gratitude is not just words; a wife shows it by her submission and her reverence. That is the desire to her husband.

It is no licence for the husband to behave however he wants. She still has to fulfil her role even when he is going off, but there is a big judgment on a man who takes the step of marriage, by the weight of his responsibility: he is the saviour of the body, and his decisions affect the whole household. The husband and the father can even disallow the vows of his wife or his daughter; that is the gravity of the position, like a rank in the church.

So the real test of submission comes when she disagrees. A wife may think she is submissive until there is something she disagrees with.

sense.text:
“Likewise, ye wives, be in subjection to your own husbands; that, if any obey not the word, they also may without the word be won by the conversation of the wives.” Conversation is not just talking. It is speech, but it is more actions than anything else, as verses 3 and 4 show: not the outward adorning, but her actions and her character.

Peter is not speaking of a husband who does everything the wife wants; he says plainly that they “obey not the word.” And did he say argue harder? Keep explaining until he understands, keep trying to convince him? Withdraw affection, give him the silent treatment, put the hands up when he reaches for her? Punish him emotionally, keep reminding him why she is upset? No. The Bible makes it about her again: her conduct is what becomes persuasive to the man.

Many modern women struggle in marriage because they have learned to explain themselves better than they have learned to examine themselves. When she is disrespectful she wants him to remember everything she has been carrying; when she is emotionally reactive she wants him to consider her stress; when she withdraws or turns cold she wants him to understand how deeply she was hurt. She wants context for herself and accountability for him. And many sisters read 1 Peter 3:1-2 and think conversation means that if she speaks to him pleasantly and melodically she can explain herself better. No.

“While they behold your chaste conversation coupled with fear.” Not that the husband is fearful: he sees her fear toward God. Despite what he is doing she still plays her role as a wife; he sees her applying the commandments for a wife, even while he is out of the spirit in that moment.

A husband should understand his wife, as we should understand why anyone does what they do, so that we are better equipped to make judgment. But it is within the construct of the order. It is not simping after her to make amends.

“Likewise, ye husbands, dwell with them according to knowledge”: treat her with understanding as you go through this thing called marriage together. Know the spirit in your wife the way you know the spirit in your kids; if you proved her, you did, and if not, you are learning on the go.

“Giving honour unto the wife, as unto the weaker vessel”: acknowledging that he is in authority, that he is the one to build her up and strengthen her. There are many layers to the weaker vessel, and one of the primary ones is how easily women are carried about by different doctrines, how persuadable they are.

“And as being heirs together of the grace of life”: back to the unity again. “That your prayers be not hindered”: because otherwise there is division in the household, place is given to the devil, and the divide widens. That doesn’t mean he gives the same energy back, and it doesn’t mean he goes chasing her to talk to him. But he shouldn’t add to it. Usually when a man is hurt he reacts like a child in his immaturity, tries to hurt her back, creates a cycle and widens the division in the home.

Her feelings matter; he is to know her, understand her and honour her. But understanding behavior is not the same thing as excusing behavior, and a husband has to know that fine line: there is accountability to be had, and that is part of dwelling with her according to knowledge. Stress can explain disrespect. Hurt can explain withdrawal. Fear can explain anger. Disappointment can explain harsh speech. But explanation is still not justification. In seeking to explain, a wife is really seeking to justify her actions, and in doing that she shames both her husband and his head, which is Christ.

If explanation were justification with God, every commandment could be excused with enough context, and that is what Christianity does. As Bishop Nathanyel says about judgments: take the feelings and the emotions out, go by what the scripture says, and it all makes sense. Understanding still doesn’t justify the behavior; the judgment still comes, because that is order. What understanding does is open the door of compassion to gain the person back. And those principles apply to the husband as well. Sisters will sit through a whole class and take only this part back to their husbands.

precepts.why:
Dividing the household gives place to the devil: “Be ye angry, and sin not: let not the sun go down upon your wrath: Neither give place to the devil.” You can be upset, but don’t let your wisdom fail. It doesn’t mean make up before you go to bed; it means don’t let your wisdom fade in your anger.

Trying to create and widen the divide is giving place to the devil. That is counsel for the husband and the wife alike: don’t let emotions cloud your judgment so that you stop ruling your house the way you need to.

sense.text:
To be better equipped to submit, a biblical woman has to examine herself. “Every wise woman buildeth her house.” When a wife withholds affection and does those things, she starts breaking down her own house. It is like a man who gets angry and breaks things in his own house, his TV, his walls, his furniture, and then has to fix it, or is so broke he lives with holes in the wall. Spiritually, she breaks down her house by creating more division, widening the gap, and making her husband go cold toward her.

If she has the wisdom she thinks she has, she builds her house, and she builds it by applying 1 Peter 3, Ephesians 5 and Proverbs 31, and going back to Genesis. Her words build him; they build confidence in him. Building the house is not only pictures on the wall and choosing the throw rug and the furniture; it is strengthening her husband, which is very different from trying to change him.

We lose meaning in the everyday, like knowing an answer and not being able to recall it. That is what meditating on verses is for: not reading it once and saying I know what it says, but truly reflecting on it until it resonates with the spirit, so that the inner man built up after Christ shows forth, not the carnal, worldly-conditioned, pre-programmed brother or sister.

So the question is not what it took to make her respond that way to the man she is to reverence and submit to as unto the Lord. It is: what am I building right now? Am I going to build, or tear down? As a wife and help meet, a pillar of rest, she doesn’t let that house get torn down, and she certainly doesn’t do it herself. That is self-examination.

“Examine yourselves, whether ye be in the faith; prove your own selves. Know ye not your own selves, how that Jesus Christ is in you, except ye be reprobates?” Christ is in you unless you are reprobate, void of God and of understanding. That spirit is there, but you have to take these steps to see which one is going to show forth in action.

precepts.why:
“But let every man prove his own work, and then shall he have rejoicing in himself alone, and not in another.” The scripture commands us to prove our own work.

This is a maturity thing. A mature believer can ask: even if I was wronged, was my response righteous? Replace asking whether you were justified in being upset with asking whether, even if you were wronged, your response was righteous, and the outbursts start to get better. That goes for brothers too, not just sisters in marriage.

You can be 100% right about the problem and wrong in your response to the problem. Again, the explanation is not justification; it doesn’t excuse it.

sense.text: “Whose adorning let it not be that outward adorning of plaiting the hair, and of wearing of gold, or of putting on of apparel”: this is why conversation is not just words but actions. After verses 1 and 2 he speaks of the outward show, and says let the adorning be the things that are in the fear of God. Not trying to win him over by looking cute and doing herself up; that is seductive, worldly and carnal.

“But let it be the hidden man of the heart, in that which is not corruptible”: Christ is in you unless you are reprobate. The outward things are carnal. Coupled with the foundation of the inner man they are all right, but many sisters sweep things under the rug: let’s just go on a date. She feels good, gets away from the problem, never addresses the elephant in the room, and lives in a fantasy that carries her a few days. The real issue is never dealt with and Satan is still in the midst of the household. She thinks she is worthy of a unified kingdom under Christ but can’t unify her own household.

“Even the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit.” Meek means gentle, not aggressive, not all up in his face. Her actions, her demeanour and her countenance should truly reflect it when she deals with her husband, “which is in the sight of God of great price.”

It goes into self-discipline: discipline and training of oneself, usually for improvement. She is accountable to train herself. Some say their husband doesn’t teach them, and that is why they act the way they do. No: a husband teaches every day by his actions, his stoicism and austerity, his nurturing, protecting and providing in the home. Self-discipline is governing your emotions, your words, your desires and your conduct, building yourself to be principled rather than impulsive. That is strength in order under God’s word, the real strength.

The meek and quiet spirit is deeply connected to submission. There is more that goes into it, but he names these two because if she focuses on them the rest will follow; righteous spirits gather together.

“For after this manner in the old time the holy women also, who trusted in God, adorned themselves, being in subjection unto their own husbands”. The key is that they trusted in God. They didn’t say he’s my project, I’m going to change him, fix him. They trusted God enough to play their role harder in times of adversity, so that God could be present in that marriage. God will deal with the husband.

“Even as Sara obeyed Abraham, calling him lord: whose daughters ye are, as long as ye do well, and are not afraid with any amazement.” Not afraid to submit, not afraid that it will run her errant. Being unyielding doesn’t make what the husband is doing right, but staying in her lane with God makes her right; and if she believes and fears God and has confidence in him, he will show her a path forward to reconciliation in the division in her house.

These things work together: the spirit of submission, understanding why we submit, then the conduct that follows (not just words), and with it meekness and quietness. And biblical submission is not eventually doing what he said after so much trifling, arguing, division and hatred. A wife can comply and still be contemptuous, sarcastic, hostile, dismissive, and have a rebellious spirit. Sarcasm is a covert way of fighting back or asserting superiority without engaging in direct conflict, and it is a disrespectful manifestation of a serious topic. Sarcasm in a funny moment together is fine; every other time it is like nails on a chalkboard. Nasty ass.

Submission is really obedience, and certain spirits accompany it. “The grace of a wife delighteth her husband, and her discretion will fatten his bones.”

Grace here is not mercy or pardon. It is favour, good will, kindness; a manifestation of favour, especially by a superior; and graciousness, being pleasantly kind, benevolent and courteous. It brings delight rather than heaviness. The grace of a wife is the pleasingness a woman can have on her husband, and it is not just looks and appearance; Peter said let it not be the outward adorning. If she wants to get into her man’s heart and show him she loves him, it is the meek and quiet spirit.

A wife thinks respect is about speaking kindly, but a husband experiences it when she trusts his leadership even when she would have chosen another path; when she doesn’t question every decision until he feels he is standing before a jury instead of beside his wife; when her words build his confidence instead of quietly dismantling it; when he knows she is for him, not against him. The whole world is against us out there; at home we aren’t trying to deal with that.

Her discretion fattens his bones: she builds him up because she doesn’t act out. She stays in the meek and quiet spirit; her chaste conversation coupled with the fear of the Lord shows all these things, and it changes how she experiences her husband in marriage. This is how she handles things whether he is in order or out of it, as in 1 Peter 3, if any obey not the word. To be discreet is to be prudent and discerning, able to speak and act with sound judgment: learning not to be sarcastic, not to be questioning, not to be disrespectful.

“A silent and loving woman is a gift of the Lord; and there is nothing so much worth as a mind well instructed.” Silence doesn’t only mean be quiet: it speaks of a mind well instructed, so her behaviours are what matter behind it. Silent is quiet and peaceable: not always arguing, not wanting to quarrel, not ruled by the need to say something. It doesn’t mean mute, though if her husband likes mute, she adapts to him.

Loving means showing affection: goodwill and devoted care to her husband, however he likes to be cared for, not the way she thinks. She has to learn that.

Well instructed means studying and meditating to build herself up, so her mind and spirit are governed by the principles and commandments of the scriptures. She cannot be a silent and loving woman if her mind is not well instructed, and that is her to learn and study, especially with the world set up as it is. She has to seek out the book and meditate on what she needs to improve in, rather than sisterhood and woman-empowerment teaching veiled as scripture.

“A shamefaced and faithful woman is a double grace, and her continent mind cannot be valued.” Shamefaced is having a proper sense of shame, not brazen; she isn’t shamefaced when she talks all extra and aggressive. Faithful goes without saying when it comes to fornication, but it means she is trustworthy, loyal and dependable to him.

A continent mind is not pulled by emotions: self-disciplined, self-controlled and restrained, especially in her appetites, her passions and her conduct. These things are on display, but they start inside, in the mind and in where her desires really are.

“As the sun when it ariseth in the high heaven; so is the beauty of a good wife in the ordering of her house.” The house is her domain. Orderly is well arranged and disciplined, including the ordering of the house. It is a rare man who is all right with a messy home; most men are built for order.

precepts.why:
“She openeth her mouth with wisdom; and in her tongue is the law of kindness.” It doesn’t say kindness; it says the law of kindness. His commandments are what come out of her mouth. That is her chaste conversation coupled with fear, and it is her requirement as a wife to her husband.

So the mind well instructed shows in the tongue: disciplined speech, against the uncontrolled, contentious tongue.

sense.text:
Verses 13 to 16 gave the righteous woman: gracious, discreet, silent, loving, well instructed, shamefaced, faithful, continent and orderly. Now the contrast, because sometimes we understand better by knowing what not to be.

“A dishonest woman contemneth shame: but an honest woman will reverence her husband.” Dishonest is lying and dealing falsely, but it is also not being honest with herself in the manipulation she brings to her marriage by trying to be the head; she ends up deceiving herself. And if she doesn’t reverence him, she is dishonest and disloyal.

“A shameless woman shall be counted as a dog; but she that is shamefaced will fear the Lord.” Christ told the Syrophenician woman he would not give the children’s bread to the dogs: it is not for you. Ephesians is about unity and how it is kept in ourselves, the congregation, the marriage and with the children. A wife who lets her house be torn down instead of building it up is counted as a dog. She can’t think she will ride into the kingdom of heaven on her husband’s righteousness or his position; once she becomes a wife in this truth she is accountable for her own actions before the Lord, her own members of sin, and her accountability to her husband and her children.

“A woman that honoureth her husband shall be judged wise of all”: she will be able to get into the kingdom of heaven. “But she that dishonoureth him in her pride shall be counted ungodly of all,” and nothing ungodly enters the gates of the kingdom of heaven. Some Christian woman will clip this and ask whether she really can’t inherit the kingdom for being like that to her husband. Yes: a woman who marries and doesn’t do what is required of her as a wife is just biding her time.

Notice it calls the lack of submission pride; not applying these things is pride.

The godly wife shows grace, discretion, is silent and loving, well instructed, shamefaced and faithful, honours her husband and orders her house (some sisters have a lazy spirit and the house is always a mess, and that is part of it too). The contrary spirit is pride, dishonour, shamelessness, loudness, scolding, contention and undisciplined speech; some sisters think they get by because they don’t do the rest, but they have undisciplined speech. So she should ask: which woman am I becoming when conflict enters my marriage? She meditates on these chapters and deals with it, and it is not taken out on her husband, nor made a qualifier for how she treats him.

Still the contrary spirit, the contentious woman: “It is better to dwell in a corner of the housetop, than with a brawling woman in a wide house.” He is in the corner of the attic to get away from her. She asks why he won’t sit with her; she needs to check how her spirit is, because he doesn’t want to be next to her. That is why brothers say, damn, I got to go home. No attic? In a one-bedroom apartment he is sitting on the corner of the couch as far away from her as possible.

precepts.why: “It is better to dwell in the corner of the housetop, than with a brawling woman and in a wide house.” Almost exactly the same words, written twice: twice so we understand that it is fact.

This is what it really looks like: “A continual dropping in a very rainy day and a contentious woman are alike.” Contentious is tending to argument or strife: quarrelsome, argumentative, disputatious. Contention from a wife is not always one big explosion.

Drip, drip, drip. Criticism, drip. Correction, drip. Complaint, drip. Sarcasm, drip. Another comment, another reminder, another explanation, drip. Then the husband blows up, and she says it came out of nowhere. It didn’t; it came from all the contentious drips. And then they paint him as the bad guy.

That continual dropping, all the complaints and criticisms of the man, makes the house toxic, a hostile environment with no peace. “For three things the earth is disquieted, and for four which it cannot bear”: when the earth is disquieted, there is no peace.

“For a servant when he reigneth”: servants are reigning over the earth today. That is why the scriptures say the earth is turned upside down; the rightful owners of the earth are not ruling, and there is no peace in the earth. “And a fool when he is filled with meat.”

“For an odious woman when she is married.” Odious is deserving or causing hatred: hateful, detestable; execrable, despicable, objectionable, abominable. Its opposites are lovable and attractive, and that is not physical attraction but the inner woman Peter spoke of. She probably got married because she looked good, but she has all these qualities about her, and an odious woman when she is married disquiets even the earth. It is the same as the housetop: better there than with the contentious woman.

sense.text:
Against the odious woman, here is what a wife is to become: “Who can find a virtuous woman? for her price is far above rubies.” Some sisters are flippant about it, saying none of us is going to be that; some say they are in training but put in none of the effort. It is something to desire in earnest, and while her price is far above rubies and she is hard to find, the same chapter tells you what to do to become her. It is the playbook, like an athlete who is told to be disciplined, arrive early and train so many times, and with the discipline and conviction becomes it.

The virtuous woman is not unobtainable in these last days, because the manual is right here. Drop the pride, stop being odious, come back to this and model yourself after it. Her mom may have been a hoe who never taught her, and there may be no good examples around her: she has it right here.

“The heart of her husband doth safely trust in her, so that he shall have no need of spoil. She will do him good and not evil all the days of her life.” That doesn’t only mean she won’t cheat on him; for a married woman that should be a given, because it is one and done: cheat on the man and you are out. Doing him good and not evil is everything spoken of up to here: the submission, the meek and quiet spirit.

“She seeketh wool, and flax, and worketh willingly with her hands.” It was a different time and things were obtained differently. The ideal is that the wife doesn’t work, but it is crazy out here, and in many cases you can’t survive without two incomes unless the man is doing exceptionally well. That still doesn’t change what the Lord requires of her.
“She is like the merchants’ ships; she bringeth her food from afar.” If she has to commute an hour each way, she commutes an hour each way. No excuses.
“She riseth also while it is yet night, and giveth meat to her household, and a portion to her maidens.” She held it down: woke up early and took care of her household and her maidens.
“She considereth a field, and buyeth it”: she has sense. She was able to be out there making important decisions, and her husband was able to trust in them.

“She girdeth her loins with strength, and strengtheneth her arms.” Not trying to be manly: she has built herself up with the scriptures and knows how to weather the emotional storm inside her so she can keep doing what she has to do.
“Her candle goeth not out by night”: the same as Ephesians 4, the sun not going down on your wrath. She doesn’t lose her wisdom when she is out of the spirit; that is no excuse.
“She layeth her hands to the spindle, and her hands hold the distaff.” She can make fringes, work, buy food and cook it. A husband’s shirts shouldn’t sit for two years before they are fringed.
“She is not afraid of the snow for her household: for all her household are clothed with scarlet.” She made provision; she knows how to handle the times, literally weathering the storm.
“Her husband is known in the gates, when he sitteth among the elders of the land”: his reputation rests on his household, which includes himself.
“Strength and honour are her clothing”: as in verse 17, she girdeth her loins with strength.

“She openeth her mouth with wisdom; and in her tongue is the law of kindness.” When she opens her mouth it is wisdom, not abrasiveness, not continual dripping. She knows how, when and in what spirit to say what she needs to say; that is what silent and loving really means.

So submission doesn’t mean a woman can’t give her husband advice. When she knows how, when, what and in what spirit, it is valuable, especially when she is involved in the body like this. Many wives, especially leadership wives, sit on their husband’s rank instead of making their own name and works. A wife who puts her hand to the plough, helps the other sisters, and brings her husband a perspective he can’t hear himself, not in a gossiping manner, becomes invaluable in building the congregation. That is how it should be.

precepts.why:
Here is the example: “And David said to Abigail, Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, which sent thee this day to meet me: And blessed be thy advice, and blessed be thou, which hast kept me this day from coming to shed blood, and from avenging myself with mine own hand.” Blessed be her advice; so a woman doesn’t have to be shut up with no advice to give.

Abigail was intelligent, decisive, articulate and courageous, and she gave David counsel that prevented bloodshed. A godly woman has a view and a perspective; she knows how to communicate wisdom without abandoning order, respect, discretion and self-control. She can say her piece, as long as she doesn’t abandon those.

What if the husband is wrong, or in sin? Subjection in all things does not mean he can tell her to sin; she obeys God. But some will use that line to refuse a husband who told them to sin, and won’t apply the laws of a wife, and so are in sin themselves. It is sin not to apply the laws for a wife: every time she is disrespectful to him, every time she speaks out of turn, every time she abandons those commandments. And there is no context that justifies sin.

sense.text:
Husbands have a judgment too. After “the husband is the head of the wife” and “so let the wives be to their own husbands in every thing,” it says: “Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it; That he might sanctify and cleanse it with the washing of water by the word”. The husband has accountability: to dwell with her according to knowledge and give honour to her as the weaker vessel.

This is the real 50/50 the Bible speaks of. The wife asks: did I submit, did I reverence, did I govern my spirit, did I speak with wisdom? The husband asks: did I love with the sacrificial love, did I understand, did I honour, did I nourish, did I cherish, did I lead the way I was supposed to? Neither gets the answer by pointing at the spouse. He can’t say, Lord, it’s the wife you gave me, and the wife can’t blame the husband.

The husband’s responsibilities, a love that gives, protects and leads, are many more and more demanding than the wife’s: sacrifice, being willing to lay down self for her; nourish her spiritual, emotional and physical well-being; cherish her, which is not putting her on a pedestal but seeing her value, treating her with care and tenderness and not like one of the brothers; lead in righteousness, because the man sets the spiritual direction of the home, not the woman; protect her and be her covering; teach and guide her by the word; love her as his own body; dwell with her according to knowledge; give her honour. The wife’s is a submission that builds, not destroys: submit, reverence, govern her spirit with a meek and quiet spirit, speak with wisdom and a tongue of kindness, and build the home, ordering her house well.

Submission is revealed under pressure. It is easy to be quiet when nothing bothers you, easy to reverence a husband you agree with, easy to be kind when you feel appreciated, easy to follow when he decides what you wanted. Meekness, submission, reverence, discretion and self-government become meaningful when she is disappointed, offended, stressed, hurt, or disagrees; that is when she needs them most, and when they will make sense. Likewise headship becomes meaningful when the wife is difficult to understand, emotional, disagreeable or disappointing, and some brothers are ready to throw her away. That is when she finds out whether she is in subjection to him, and he finds out whether he is in subjection to Christ.

“Finally, my brethren”: this is the closing of the letter. After everything coming under one in Christ, one body, one new man, the middle wall of partition down, then husbands and wives, children and parents, servants and masters, congregational issues and us as individuals, he says, “be strong in the Lord, and in the power of his might.”

These verses are about the unity God creates under Christ. Endeavouring to keep the unity of the spirit in the bond of peace means it has to be defended, because Satan wants to come for that unity. He doesn’t want us united in Christ; lies, bitterness, accusations, temptations and divisions are all going to come.

“Put on the whole armour of God, that ye may be able to stand against the wiles of the devil. For we wrestle not against flesh and blood”. It is true that we wrestle against the evil governments, religions and world order, but in the context of this letter he is reminding us who the enemy is. The enemy is not your spouse, not your children, not the brother and sister next to you, not the northern kingdom, not those who lived as Gentiles, not the Jews who lived right and vexed you. The enemy comes at us spiritually.

Christ said a man’s foes will be them of his own household, but that is when belief in him divides a family: those who won’t believe on him the way the scriptures say become the enemy, because they will try to divide you from him. If anything that reinforces what Paul is saying. We have to hold up that oneness in Christ: stand for the brotherhood, for ourselves as individuals, and not only for our own marriages but for marriage itself in a world where fornication and whoremongering are heavy on the earth; that is the only reason trad wives are even a thing.

“Wherefore take unto you the whole armour of God, that ye may be able to withstand in the evil day, and having done all, to stand.” In English “you” can be singular or plural, and here “ye” is plural: he is talking to us as a body. Each one individually puts it on, and together we are all wearing armour and stronger. It is not one person’s job; all of us should be of this mind to defend the unity. That is endeavouring to keep the unity of the spirit.

“Stand therefore, having your loins girt about with truth”. He uses the armour as a similitude because they were under Rome, with Roman soldiers everywhere, so it was relatable even to those who weren’t warriors. A Roman soldier’s belt secured his equipment; in marriage and community, truth and integrity keep everything from coming apart. Lie not one to another; don’t deal falsely with one another; speak truth to your neighbour. Lies and liars can destroy everything that has been built, and we should not have that among ourselves.

“And having on the breastplate of righteousness”: the breastplate guards the vital organs in the centre, the heart and the lungs. Righteous conduct protects the heart of the family against bitterness, malice and unfaithfulness. Don’t let those creep in.

“And your feet shod with the preparation of the gospel of peace”: Roman military footwear had grips on the bottom to keep firm footing. Peace keeps the family from constantly slipping into conflict; we keep the unity by gripping onto it with peace. He is not just saying put on a belt or a breastplate; he relates each piece to principles of the truth, spirits we must strive to keep individually, as a body, in marriages and with our children.

“Above all, taking the shield of faith, wherewith ye shall be able to quench all the fiery darts of the wicked.” Shields protect the individual, but in the phalanx, the Roman testudo, unified shields made a wall, a shell, an armed body of believers, like the shell of shields in the movie 300. That is the picture against the fiery darts of division, doubt and accusation, everything that divides us: everybody keep their shield.

“And take the helmet of salvation”: the helmet guards the head. Salvation protects the mind against thoughts and anxiety that warp how you see God, yourself and one another. You start to surmise, to see evil in a brother, to build hatred and bitterness, and if it is never resolved because the helmet was off, it shows in the breaking of the union, the unity, the fellowship; depending on where it is caught, it can be a travesty.

“And the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God”: the word of God exposes and strikes down lies.

“Praying always with all prayer and supplication in the Spirit”: pray for these things, pray for unity, and pray to see what is wrong in yourself. “And watching thereunto with all perseverance and supplication for all saints”: for all of us. The family should not be fighting each other while the enemy is shooting at all of us.

This world is polluted, and its destruction is real. People are talking about Lindsay Clancy, the baby killer, whose supporters say that when she was stressed and bugged out she was justified in killing her children. If she is retried and found innocent, lawyers are advising men to put language about it in their prenups, and in a custody battle a mother who publicly supported her can be shown to put the children’s welfare in danger. Men are calling off weddings over it. One man broke it off two weeks out, not over an opinion but because that opinion showed a fundamental difference in values: he could have compassion for someone struggling mentally without excusing what happened to those children, and he needed to trust completely the judgment of the woman who might be the mother of his children. Good for him. Values matter more than liking the same food or the same music.

Submission, grace, self-examination, marriage, unity and the armour of God all come together. The wife must examine whether she is governed by the word when pressure enters the marriage. The husband must examine whether he is loving and leading like Christ. And the whole household must remember that they are called to stand together under Christ against a common enemy, and it is not each other. That unity is only present with the right order and structure, carried from marriage to parenting to the congregation to how we deal with one another. Whoever is against that order is against what God wills for us to have together, to protect us from the evil out there.

precepts.why:
The sword of the Spirit is the word of God: “For the word of God is quick, and powerful, and sharper than any twoedged sword, piercing even to the dividing asunder of soul and spirit”. It casts down lies and shows where the truth is, because lies fracture relationships.

“And of the joints and marrow, and is a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart.” We must live by it. When those feelings and thoughts come out, when she is rebellious to submission, she must use the word of God, not the Instagram sister who is miserable, living a fantasy online, and trying to guide her relationship so she can classify her man and put him in a box.

And the word shows the thoughts and intents, not of someone else’s heart, but your own. It is for you to examine yourself whether you be in the faith, as at the start of the class. Christ is in you unless you are reprobate, void of God and understanding, talking about living by the word of God and not doing it.
